title: Human language (Guide 1:26)
hookLine: the Torah speaks in human language

lines: TRUE, IN WORDS A CHILD CAN HOLD.
A DOOR THAT OPENS ON TIME.
cards: A four-year-old asks where the sun goes at night. The parent doesn't open with orbits and the turning of the earth. They say something like: the sun goes to sleep on the other side of the world.
It isn't a lie. It's the truth, said in words a four-year-old can hold. Later the child will learn more, and the first answer won't feel like a trick.
It'll feel like a door that opened on time. A phrase from the rabbis says the Torah does something like this.

teach.b: Human language. In Hebrew, dibrah Torah kilshon b'nei adam: the Torah speaks in the language of human beings. First, where it starts.
The phrase comes from the Talmud, where some rabbis use it in arguments about how to read a verse: don't squeeze a hidden lesson out of every doubled word, because people talk that way.
Second, what Maimonides does with it. In chapter twenty-six of the Guide's first part, he gives the phrase a bigger job.

The Torah speaks so everyone can understand it, including people who aren't philosophers. And people at large, he says, can only picture something as real if it's a body, something that moves, acts, lives.
So the Torah describes God with words like those: God sees, speaks, comes down, is alive. Third, an example.

teach.h: THE LORD CAME DOWN TO SEE.
teach.b: At Babel, the verse says, "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." To Maimonides, this isn't a report about travel. It's human words saying that God attends to what people do.

teach.h: HOLDING THE TEXT WITH BOTH HANDS.
teach.b: This one phrase lets a reader hold the text with both hands: honoring every word, and still reading the words as speech meant for people. That was the relief the Guide offered the perplexed student.

teach.h: THE TORAH SPEAKS IN HUMAN LANGUAGE.
teach.b: Now look back over this week: a loan or a job, so nobody needs to ask; giving where neither knows; the path of return; you can be Moses; a world at peace; a book for the perplexed; and a Torah that speaks our language.

how: Jews who study the Guide often read its opening chapters alongside the verses they discuss, asking of each bodily word for God what it figuratively means. The phrase 'the Torah speaks in human language' is also a familiar principle in classical commentary.

games.q: you're reading Genesis with a student. the verse says, "the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." the student asks: did God travel? how does Maimonides read it?
o: yes, God moved from one place to another.
it's human language for God attending to what people do.
games.why: for Maimonides the Torah speaks in human language: 'came down to see' says that God attends, not that God travels.

practice: Bring to mind a verse with God's hand, or eyes, or walking, or speaking in it, and say it to yourself slowly. Then ask: if this is a figure of speech, what is it saying in plain terms, care, power, attention?
Let the picture stay a picture, and let the meaning come up underneath it.

wordCard.voice: Human language. The rabbinic phrase that the Torah speaks in the language of human beings, which Maimonides uses to read the Torah's bodily words for God as speech meant for people. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the torah speaks our language. True words, fitted to the people who hear them. Another week, done.
